notes.body:
Within every prayer (صلاة) is a moment of intimate recitation — the seated testimony (التشهد) performed in the final position of the prayer. Nestled inside it is a **salaam directed toward the Prophet and the congregation**: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings; peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah." This is the salaam of the remembrance (سلام الذكر) — a salaam spoken from inside the sanctuary of the prayer, not one that opens its door.

The closing salaam (التسليم), by contrast, is the act that **ends the prayer entirely**. When a worshipper turns and says السلام عليكم, they step out of the state of ritual consecration and back into ordinary life. Think of the prayer as a sealed room of communion: the salaam of the remembrance (سلام الذكر) is a word of peace uttered inside that room, while التسليم is the act of opening the door and leaving.

This distinction carries real legal force in the passage we are reading. A follower has declared his intent to follow the Imam, but by the time the Imam reaches the salaam of the remembrance (سلام الذكر), the follower has not yet truly formed his intention (النية) in his heart. The answer turns on whether the **Imam carries the intention on the follower's behalf**: if the Imam does, the prayer stands; if not, it lapses. The Imam is not merely a leader in posture — he is a spiritual custodian whose sincerity can shelter the whole congregation.

Because the salaam of the remembrance (سلام الذكر) does not seal the prayer, **a window still exists**. The follower can still align his heart before التسليم arrives and shuts the gate. Maulana Ali taught that doubt does not erase certainty — and the law does not rush to invalidate a prayer that still has life in it.

etymology: الذكر (remembrance): from the root ذ-ك-ر, meaning to remember and to mention aloud — a union the tradition treats as inseparable. Memory here is never silent; to truly remember something is to voice it. The noun الذكر names any act that keeps something alive through both heart and tongue working together.

السلام (peace): from the root س-ل-م, whose core sense is wholeness, safety, and freedom from harm. The verb سَلِمَ means to be intact and undamaged. When the worshipper says السلام, they offer not merely a greeting but a declaration — an extension of the state of being whole to another.

التسليم (the closing salaam): also from س-ل-م, but cast in the intensive Form II pattern, giving it a causative force: to bestow peace, to hand it outward. التسليم is the act of releasing peace across the threshold — the worshipper gives peace away and, in that giving, formally steps outside the prayer.

التشهد (the testimony): from the root ش-ه-د, to witness and to be present. الشاهد is the witness; الشهادة is testimony. التشهد is the act of bearing witness — placing oneself before truth and declaring it aloud — making the seated recitation a living moment of witnessing the divine.

notes.body:
When the text speaks of "a surah taken from above," it is describing the **Quran's own sequence** as it runs from beginning to end. The surahs at the start — Al-Fatiha, Al-Baqarah, and those that follow — sit "above," while the shorter surahs near the end, like Al-Ikhlas and An-Nas, sit "below." So if a worshipper recites Al-Ikhlas in the first unit (ركعة) of prayer and then, in the second, reaches back to Al-Kawthar — which appears earlier in the Quran — they have taken a surah "from above."

The practice expected here is called **ordering** (ترتيب): the surah of the second rakah should follow, not precede, the surah of the first. Think of it as reading a book — we would not flip back to an earlier chapter after having already moved past it.

The prostration of omission is not stipulated for this mistake — the prayer stands. But the text adds: "he should not do it deliberately," marking the act as **disliked**, something that falls short of the beauty we owe to prayer without breaking it.

It belongs to the etiquette (أدب) of worship, not to the **pillars** (أركان). This same spirit runs through the earlier ruling, where reciting prayer "in reverse order, from bottom to top" also carries no obligation for the prostration of omission. Together, these rulings affirm that the Quran's order shapes the dignity of our prayer, yet Allah, in His mercy, does not hold the inattentive worshipper to the same account as one who misses a pillar.

etymology: ترتيب (ordering): from the root ر-ت-ب, meaning to place things in fixed ranks or rows. The noun رَتْبَة is a rank or grade. ترتيب is the act of establishing that sequence — connecting directly to prayer, where the surahs recited across rakahs are expected to follow the Quran's own ranked order from beginning to end.

ركعة (unit of prayer): from the root ر-ك-ع, meaning to bow or incline the body forward. A ركعة is one complete unit of prayer, named after its most distinctive physical act — the bow of humility before Allah. The root locks the name to the posture that gives the unit its identity.

أدب (etiquette): from the root أ-د-ب, whose earliest sense was to invite others to a feast or gathering. Over time it came to mean cultivated and refined conduct. In religious law, أدب names acts that are beautiful and proper in worship — honourable and recommended, though not obligatory pillars.

أركان (pillars): from the root ر-ك-ن, meaning a corner or load-bearing support. The singular رُكْن is a cornerstone. In prayer, الأركان are the foundational acts — bowing and prostration among them — that bear the structure of the prayer upright. Remove them, and the edifice falls.

notes.body:
The two cases pivot on a single difference: **how many rakahs are genuinely uncertain.** When we doubt between three and four, only one rakah hangs in the balance; when we doubt between two and four, two full rakahs are unknown.

A seated rakah carries a lighter legal weight than a standing one — sufficient to repair a gap of one, yet too light to corrupt a prayer that needed no repair at all. If the prayer was already complete at four, the seated rakahs become voluntary prayer appended at the end; if it was truly at three, they provide the **cautious completion** the prayer needs.

When the uncertain gap is two full rakahs, seated rakahs would not suffice — the obligatory prayer requires **full standing rakahs** to restore its structure. If the prayer was already at four, those two standing rakahs become voluntary; if only two were prayed, they complete the prayer properly.

Two rules hold across both cases:

- The remedial rakahs are performed after the salaam, so the obligatory prayer is formally closed before they begin — any error in the remedy cannot reach back and corrupt it.
- The prostrations of omission (سجدتا السهو) follow in both cases, formally sealing the uncertainty.

This flows from Maulana Ali's teaching — that doubt neither dispels certainty nor diminishes it; we **act on what we know** and supply what remains in a form precisely sized to protect the prayer's obligatory core.

notes.quote: he delivers the salaam, prays two rakahs seated, and performs the two prostrations of omission
etymology: سهو (omission): from the root س-ه-و, meaning to slip inadvertently in awareness or to drift from attention. The root conveys a quiet, unintentional wandering of the mind — not wilful neglect but a moment when focus simply was not there. سهو names this unguarded lapse, and the derived word stays faithful to that image of attention quietly slipping away.

شك (doubt): from the root ش-ك-ك, meaning to pierce something through, dividing it. When two possibilities simultaneously run through the mind and split it — neither resolved, neither dispelled — that divided state is شك. The image is of something cut cleanly in two: certainty has been severed, and the mind sits suspended between the two halves.

notes.body:
The chapter presents both reports back to back; the discomfort a reader feels is intentional — that is where the teaching lives. The first says that a woman, a donkey, and a black dog are among those things that interrupt the prayer (صلاة). The second is the Prophet's own lived response.

ثَلَاثٌ تَقْطَعُ الصَّلَاةَ الْمَرْأَةُ وَالْحِمَارُ وَالْكَلْبُ الْأَسْوَدُ
Three things interrupt the prayer: a woman, a donkey, and a black dog.

All three passed before the Prophet while he was praying. He did not stop or begin again; he completed his worship, and when it was done, he turned to those watching and said:

رَأَيْتُ الَّذِي رَأَيْتُمْ وَلَيْسَ يَقْطَعُ صَلَاةَ الْمُؤْمِنِ شَيْءٌ وَلَكِنِ ادْرَءُوا مَا اسْتَطَعْتُمْ
I saw what you saw, and nothing interrupts the prayer of a believer; but ward off what you are able to ward off.

The Prophet himself is the reconciliation — his action and word establish that **the prayer of a believer is legally unbroken**. What the first report describes is not a legal verdict but a spiritual warning — these are forces powerful enough to shatter a worshipper's inner presence, to pull the heart away from Allah at the very moment it should be most still.

Think of a candle flame caught in a sudden gust of wind. The flame trembles, flickers, nearly disappears — but it does not go out. These three things are that gust.

The phrase "ward off what you are able" is the bridge between the two reports. It is a counsel of care, not a legal command. Protect the sacred space of worship with every means available — not because the prayer will otherwise be void, but because what is at stake is its **depth and sincerity before Allah**.

Maulana Ali brings the same reasoning to another situation:

لَا يَقْطَعُ الصَّلَاةَ التَّبَسُّمُ وَيَقْطَعُهَا الْقَهْقَهَةُ
Smiling does not interrupt the prayer, but loud laughter interrupts it.

The tradition draws a clear and repeated line between disturbance and legal disruption. A passing shadow disturbs the heart; a burst of uncontrolled laughter breaks the act itself.

notes.quote: Three things interrupt the prayer: a woman, a donkey, and a black dog
etymology: تقطع (to interrupt): from the root ق-ط-ع, meaning to cut or sever cleanly — like a blade through rope. The image is sharp and final. Derivatives include قطعة (a piece cut off) and قاطع (decisive, cutting). In the prayer context, it names an act severed so completely that it cannot simply continue where it left off.

التبسم (smiling): from the root ب-س-م, meaning to smile gently. The root suggests a slight, soft opening — a parting without force. This mildness is built into the word itself, which is why the tradition sets it so clearly apart from القهقهة. What ب-س-م names is controlled, inward, and still compatible with the state of worship.

القهقهة (loud laughter): built on the quadrilateral root ق-ه-ق-ه, a reduplicated form that mimics the sound of the act — a burst repeated and echoed in the throat. Arabic roots that double their elements often signal intensity or uncontrolled repetition. The very structure of this word captures why it breaks prayer: it is sound that overflows and cannot be contained.
